function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: Generates a Dockerfile in the specified repository directory with a default configuration. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the repository directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory name within the filesystem.

base_image.description: The base image to use in the Dockerfile. For example, 'python:3.8-slim'.

maintainer.description: The maintainer information to be added to the Dockerfile. Format should be 'Name <email@example.com>'.

port.description: The port number that the container will expose. For example, '80' for a web server.

commands.description: Additional commands to be executed when building the image, separated by ';'. For example, 'apt-get update; apt-get install -y git'.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be a valid path relative to the project root.

deployment_name.description: The name to assign to the Kubernetes deployment. This name must be unique within the Kubernetes namespace.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to use for the deployment. This should include the repository name and tag, if applicable, in the format 'repository/image:tag'.

replicas.description: The number of instances to deploy for the specified Docker image.

service_type.description: The type of service to create for the deployment. Typical values include 'ClusterIP', 'NodePort', and 'LoadBalancer'.

port.description: The port number that the service should expose. This should correspond to the port that the application inside the Docker container is set to listen on.

target_port.description: The target port on the pod to which the service will send requests. This should be the same as the port that the application inside the Docker container is set to listen on.

function.name: analyse_repo_contents
function.description: Analyzes the contents of a repository to determine the predominant programming language used within. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the repository is located. This should be the root directory of the repository.

include_subdirectories.description: A flag indicating whether to include subdirectories in the analysis. If set to true, all subdirectories will be recursively analyzed.

excluded_files.description: An array of file names or patterns to exclude from the analysis, such as ['README.md', '*.txt'].

language_threshold.description: The percentage threshold for a language to be considered predominant in the repository. This should be a value between 0 and 100. This is a float type value.

message.content:
Below is a **step‑by‑step guide** you can copy‑paste into your terminal (or adapt to your own tooling).  
I’ll walk through each numbered step, give you the exact file contents you’ll need, and explain what each part does.  

> ⚠️ **Important** – I can’t actually run `git clone`, `git push`, or any other command that touches your remote repository.  
> The snippets below are ready‑to‑use, but you’ll still have to execute them yourself on your machine or CI system.

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the repository

```bash
# Make sure you have SSH access set up for GitHub
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

If you prefer HTTPS:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse the repository & generate artefacts

### 2.1 Create / update a Dockerfile

A minimal, production‑ready Dockerfile for a typical Node.js app looks like this:

```Dockerfile
# 2.1.1 Dockerfile
# ------------------------------------
# Use the official lightweight Node.js image
FROM node:20-alpine AS builder

# Set working directory
WORKDIR /app

# Copy dependency manifests
COPY package*.json ./

# Install only production dependencies
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Copy source code
COPY . .

# Expose the port your app listens on
EXPOSE 3000

# Start the application
CMD ["node", "src/index.js"]
```

> **Why this Dockerfile?**  
> * `node:20-alpine` is small, secure, and includes the latest LTS Node.js release.  
> * `npm ci` guarantees reproducible builds.  
> * We expose port `3000` because most Node.js starter projects listen on that port (adjust if yours uses something else).

> **Tip:** If your entry point isn’t `src/index.js`, change the `CMD` line accordingly.

### 2.2 Generate Kubernetes YAML files

Create a file called `k8s/deployment.yaml` (you may need to create the `k8s` directory first):

```yaml
# 2.2.1 k8s/deployment.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest   # <-- replace with your registry/tag
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-service
spec:
  type: LoadBalancer          # Change to NodePort or ClusterIP if you don’t have an external LB
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80                  # Port exposed to the world
    targetPort: 3000          # Port inside the pod
```

> **What this does**  
> * Deploys two replicas of your app.  
> * Exposes a LoadBalancer service on port 80 that forwards traffic to port 3000 inside the pods.  
> * Adjust `image:` to point at the registry you’ll push to (e.g., Docker Hub, GHCR, ECR).

### 2.3 Create a GitHub Actions workflow

Create `.github/workflows/ci-cd.yml`:

```yaml
# 2.3.1 .github/workflows/ci-cd.yml
name: CI/CD

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  build-and-deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: production

    steps:
    - name: Checkout code
      uses: actions/checkout@v4

    - name: Set up Docker Buildx
      uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3

    - name: Log in to GitHub Container Registry
      uses: docker/login-action@v3
      with:
        registry: ghcr.io
        username: ${{ github.actor }}
        password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

    - name: Build and push Docker image
      uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
      with:
        context: .
        file: Dockerfile
        push: true
        tags: ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}:latest

    - name: Set up kubectl
      uses: azure/setup-kubectl@v3
      with:
        version: 'latest'

    - name: Apply Kubernetes manifests
      env:
        KUBECONFIG_DATA: ${{ secrets.KUBECONFIG_BASE64 }}
      run: |
        echo "$KUBECONFIG_DATA" | base64 -d > kubeconfig
        export KUBECONFIG=$PWD/kubeconfig
        kubectl apply -f k8s/deployment.yaml
```

> **Key points**  
> * Uses the built‑in `GITHUB_TOKEN` to log in to GHCR.  
> * Builds the image from the Dockerfile you just created.  
> * Pushes to `ghcr.io/<owner>/<repo>:latest`.  
> * Applies the Kubernetes manifest.  
> * You’ll need to store your cluster’s kubeconfig (base64‑encoded) in a secret named `KUBECONFIG_BASE64`.

---

## 3️⃣ Add all changed files to Git

```bash
git add Dockerfile k8s/deployment.yaml .github/workflows/ci-cd.yml
```

> If you created any new directories (`k8s`, `.github/workflows`) Git will automatically track them.

---

## 4️⃣ Commit and push

```bash
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and CI/CD workflow"
git push origin main
```

> After pushing, GitHub Actions will automatically trigger the workflow defined in `.github/workflows/ci-cd.yml`.  
> Watch the “Actions” tab to see the pipeline run.

---

## Quick sanity check

Once the workflow finishes, verify that the image exists in GHCR:

```bash
docker pull ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest
```

And confirm the deployment is live:

```bash
kubectl get deployments
kubectl get services
```

If you’re using a cloud provider (EKS, GKE, AKS), make sure your `KUBECONFIG_BASE64` secret contains the correct kubeconfig data.

---

### Recap of the files you now have

| Path | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| `Dockerfile` | Builds a lightweight Node.js image |
| `k8s/deployment.yaml` | Deploys the app to Kubernetes |
| `.github/workflows/ci-cd.yml` | Automates build, push, and deploy on pushes to `main` |

Feel free to tweak the replica count, service type, or image tag strategy (e.g., use Git SHA instead of `latest`). Happy deploying!
